summary: An experimental document that specifies ICMP messages for reporting failures when using the IP security protocols AH and ESP, such as when a packet fails authentication or decryption.

plainLanguage.summary:
If a packet arrives encrypted or authenticated and the receiving host cannot make sense of it, this RFC defines the message the host sends back to say what went wrong.

The message names the kind of failure and carries back enough of the original packet for the sender to recognise which packet it was.

questions: what is the icmp security failures message
what icmp type is security failures
subtitle: The ICMP message a host sends back when a packet protected by IPsec cannot be accepted.

tldr.problem: When a packet protected by the IP security protocols cannot be processed, the sender gets no explanation, so there is no way to tell a misconfiguration from an attempt to break in.
tldr.mechanism: A new ICMP message type, 40, carries a code saying what went wrong: an unknown or expired SPI, a failed authentication, decompression or decryption check, or a lack of authentication or authorization. It echoes the original headers and the first 64 bits of the payload so the sender can match it to what it sent.
tldr.outcome: The message lets an operator see that a security association needs reconfiguring, and lets the peer's own key management notice the failure. The document is Experimental and has not been obsoleted.

facts.label: Original payload carried back
facts.value: The first 64 bits, 8 octets, of the remaining payload data

facts.label: Reserved field
facts.value: Two octets, zero when transmitted and ignored when received

facts.label: Pointer field
facts.value: Two octets, an offset locating the most significant octet of the offending SPI

facts.label: Errors answered with an error
facts.value: None; the message is silently discarded

today: RFC 2521 is an Experimental document from March 1999 and has not been obsoleted. Its History section says the specification is stable, that it was forwarded to the IESG as a Proposed Standard in March 1996, and that there have been several implementations.

sections.title: Why a Security Failure Message Is Needed
sections.content:
This mechanism is intended for use with the Internet Security Protocols for authentication and privacy. For statically configured Security Associations, these messages indicate that the operator needs to manually reconfigure, or is attempting an unauthorized operation. They may also be used to trigger automated session-key management.

The datagram format and basic facilities are already defined for ICMP. Up-to-date values of the ICMP Type field are specified in the most recent Assigned Numbers document, and this document concerns the value 40, Security Failures.
sections.plainLanguage: Without a message like this, a sender whose protected packet is rejected has no idea whether the far end is misconfigured or someone is probing it.

sections.title: The Message Format
sections.content:
The message follows the ordinary ICMP shape: a Type field, a Code field and a Checksum, followed by a Reserved field, a Pointer field and the original Internet headers with 64 bits of payload. The Type is 40. The Code indicates the kind of failure. The Checksum is two octets and holds the ICMP checksum. The Reserved field is two octets, for future use; it MUST be set to zero when transmitted and MUST be ignored when received. The Pointer field is two octets holding an offset into the Original Internet Headers that locates the most significant octet of the offending SPI, and is zero when no SPI is present.

The Original Internet Headers field holds the original Internet Protocol header, any intervening headers up to and including the offending SPI if any, plus the first 64 bits, that is 8 octets, of the remaining payload data. This data is used by the host to match the message to the appropriate process. If a payload protocol uses port numbers, they are assumed to be in the first 64 bits of the original datagram's payload.
sections.plainLanguage: The message is the standard ICMP header plus a pointer to the part of the packet that caused the trouble, and enough of the original packet for the sender to work out which packet it was talking about.

sections.title: The Six Failure Codes
sections.content:
Code 0 is Bad SPI, which indicates that a received datagram includes a Security Parameters Index that is invalid or has expired.

Code 1 is Authentication Failed, which indicates that a received datagram failed the authenticity or integrity check for a given SPI. The RFC notes that the SPI may indicate an outer Encapsulating Security Protocol when a separate Authentication Header SPI is hidden inside.

Code 2 is Decompression Failed, which indicates that a received datagram failed a decompression check for a given SPI. Code 3 is Decryption Failed, which indicates that a received datagram failed a decryption check for a given SPI.

Code 4 is Need Authentication, which indicates that a received datagram will not be accepted without additional authentication. In this case either no SPI is present, or an unsuitable SPI is present; the RFC gives the example of an encryption SPI without integrity arriving from a secure operating system with mutually suspicious users.

Code 5 is Need Authorization, which indicates that a received datagram will not be accepted because it has insufficient authorization. In this case an authentication SPI is present that is inappropriate for the target transport or application, and the principal party denoted by the SPI does not have proper authorization for the facilities used by the datagram. The example given is a party authorized for Telnet access but not for FTP access.
sections.plainLanguage: Six codes cover the cases: the key was not recognised, the check on the packet failed at one of three stages, the packet arrived without enough protection, or the sender was not allowed to use that service.

sections.title: Error Procedures
sections.content:
As is usual with ICMP messages, upon receipt of one of these error messages that is uninterpretable or otherwise contains an error, no ICMP error message is sent in response; instead, the message is silently discarded. However, for diagnosis of problems, a node SHOULD provide the capability of logging the error, including the contents of the silently discarded datagram, and SHOULD record the event in a statistics counter.

On receipt, special care MUST be taken that the ICMP message actually includes information that matches a previously sent IP datagram. Otherwise, this might provide an opportunity for a denial of service attack.

The sending implementation MUST be able to limit the rate at which these messages are generated. The rate limit parameters SHOULD be configurable, and how the limits are applied, such as by destination or per interface, is left to the implementor's discretion.
sections.plainLanguage: A failure message is never answered with another failure message, it is just dropped and logged. The sender has to rate-limit how many it produces, and the receiver has to check that the message really is about a packet it sent.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
When a prior Security Association between the parties has not expired, these messages SHOULD be sent with authentication. However, the node MUST NOT dynamically establish a new Security Association for the sole purpose of authenticating these messages. Automated key management is computationally intensive, and this could be used for a very serious denial of service attack: it would be very easy to swamp a target with bogus SPIs from random IP sources and have it start up numerous useless key management sessions to authentically inform the putative sender.

In the event of loss of state, such as a system crash, the node will need to send failure messages to all parties that attempt subsequent communication, and in that case the node may have lost the key management technique that was used to establish the Security Association. The RFC says it is much better to simply let the peers know that there was a failure and let them request key management as needed, at their staggered timeouts. They will remember the previous key management technique and restart gracefully, which distributes the restart burden among systems and helps allow the recently failed node to manage its computational resources.

In addition, these messages inform the recipient when the ICMP sender is under attack. Unlike other ICMP error messages, they provide sufficient data to determine that they are in response to previously sent messages. It is therefore imperative that the recipient accept both authenticated and unauthenticated failure messages, and that the recipient's log indicate when the ICMP messages are not validated and when they are not in response to a valid previous message.

There is some concern that sending these messages may result in a leak of security information. For example, an attacker might use these messages to test or verify potential forged keys. However, this information is already available through the simple expedient of using Echo facilities, or waiting for a TCP three-way handshake. The rate limiting mechanism also limits this form of leak, as many messages will not result in an error indication, and at the very least it lengthens the time factor for verifying such information.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules exist to stop the message becoming a weapon. A host must not start a whole key negotiation just to sign a failure notice, because that would let an attacker tie it up with rubbish, and the receiver has to accept failure messages even when they cannot be authenticated.

viz.caption: The rules that keep these messages from being a weapon (RFC 2521, Security Considerations)

items.title: Do not answer an error with an error
items.text: An ICMP message that is uninterpretable or otherwise in error is silently discarded rather than answered.

items.title: Check that it matches something you sent
items.text: Special care must be taken that the ICMP message includes information matching a previously sent IP datagram, or it could be used for a denial of service attack.

items.title: Limit the rate
items.text: The sending implementation must be able to limit the rate at which these messages are generated, and the parameters should be configurable.

items.title: Do not start key management to sign them
items.text: A node must not dynamically establish a new Security Association for the sole purpose of authenticating these messages, since that could swamp a target with useless sessions.

items.title: Accept both kinds
items.text: The recipient must accept both authenticated and unauthenticated failure messages, and its log should say when a message was not validated.
